network.target_molecule: Arginine, stereochemically unspecified; racemic product expected
network.overall_strategy: The supplied evidence does not justify ten chemically distinct, complete prebiotic pathways. Accordingly, this graph contains one explicitly conditional candidate rather than padding the pathway count with duplicate stoichiometries or unsupported alternatives. It corrects the review's atom balances, distinguishes reductive chemistry from hydrolysis, and represents cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile conversion through carbonyl/imine equilibria rather than direct displacement of hydroxide. Early guanidination avoids requiring selective guanidination of ornithine or an unprotected four-carbon aminoaldehyde. Direct acid hydrolysis avoids the additional uncertainties of hydantoin decarbamoylation. The decisive reductions remain unvalidated: an explicit, hypothetical copper-consuming model closes their electron balances by forming Cu2S. This bookkeeping does not establish their thermodynamics, kinetics, or selectivity. All numerical conditions below are proposed screening windows, not experimental procedures established by Patel et al. (2015). Neither a demonstrated complete synthesis nor ten validated routes can be claimed from the supplied review. Neutral molecular formulas are used for bookkeeping; aqueous protonation states and catalytic proton transfers are implicit. The schema lacks a coproduct role, so Cu2S is classified as an intermediate although it is a terminal inorganic coproduct.

reactions.name: Copper(I)-assisted hydrocyanation of acetylene
agents: Copper(I) chloride/cyanide complexes in a sulfide-poor aqueous compartment

conditions.catalyst: Copper(I) complexes; active speciation must be established
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 3-6, dissolved Cu(I) 0.1-5 mM, HCN 1-20 mM, maintained acetylene supply, 1-72 h. Use a shaded, sulfide-poor compartment. Measure volatile losses and polymer formation; these are not reported optimized conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted activation of acetylene permits net addition of HCN across its triple bond. This should not be represented as facile attack of cyanide on an intrinsically electrophilic, unactivated acetylene molecule.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review attributes this connection to Patel et al. (2015). Copper-assisted acetylene hydrocyanation is chemically recognizable, but the review supplies no reaction-level operating window. The proposed conditions therefore remain unvalidated. Sulfide must be excluded during this stage because copper-sulfide precipitation can remove the soluble copper species; subsequent sulfide chemistry cannot be assumed compatible in one pot.

reactions.name: Ammonia conjugate addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9.5-11, acrylonitrile 1-10 mM, ammonia 0.1-1 M, 6-168 h. Slow delivery of acrylonitrile into an ammonia-rich reservoir is a selectivity hypothesis, not an established geological concentration schedule.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds at the beta carbon of acrylonitrile, followed by proton transfer to give 3-aminopropanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the aza-Michael reaction described in the supplied review under Patel et al. (2015). The reaction class is credible, but secondary cyanoethylation of the product amine and acrylonitrile polymerization compete. Ammonia excess may suppress multiple addition, although achievable concentrations and substrate-specific yields are not established by the supplied evidence.

reactions.name: Early guanidination with cyanamide

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.5-10.5, aminonitrile 1-10 mM, cyanamide 5-50 mM, 1-14 days. Test shaded concentrating pools separately from sulfide-rich stages. Quantify cyanamide hydrolysis, oligomerization, and substrate cyclization.

reactions.mechanism: The primary amine attacks the electrophilic carbon of cyanamide. Proton transfers produce the substituted guanidine without requiring a leaving group.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review assigns this transformation to Patel et al. (2015), but does not provide substrate-specific kinetics or yields. Early guanidination is preferable within this candidate because it avoids the unresolved alpha-versus-side-chain selectivity of ornithine guanidination. It does not establish that cyanamide concentrations or reaction selectivity were sufficient on early Earth.

reactions.name: Unvalidated copper-consuming reductive hydrolysis and cyclization
agents: Native copper, represented by mol_007, as a hypothetical stoichiometric reductant

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 6-9, substrate 0.1-5 mM, total dissolved sulfide 1-20 mM, copper loading 4-20 molar equivalents, 1-72 h. Compare dark controls with a laboratory 254 nm screen at 0.1-1 mW/cm2; that monochromatic test is not a sunlight-performance claim. Measure copper oxidation states, sulfide phases, passivation, and organic products.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized two-electron reduction of the nitrile to an imine, hydrolysis to the corresponding aldehyde with ammonia release, and intramolecular hemiaminal formation. Formal closure requires two Cu atoms oxidized to Cu(I) in one Cu2S unit; H2S supplies sulfur and hydrogen, not an unspecified catalytic electron source.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE substrate-specific transformation. The review attributes Cu/H2S-assisted cyclic-product formation to Patel et al. (2015), but its listed equations omit the necessary reduction and sometimes the oxygen source. This balanced copper-consuming model is a proposed correction, not a verified mechanism from that paper. Sulfide trapping of copper is plausible, but does not demonstrate productive nitrile reduction. Passivation, overreduction, and competing hydrolysis remain decisive bottlenecks. The three review variants are not counted as separate pathways.

reactions.name: Cyanide trapping through a cyclic-hemiaminal/open-aldehyde equilibrium

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9, cyclic substrate 0.1-5 mM, HCN 5-50 mM, 1-48 h. Establish the open-chain aldehyde fraction experimentally. After the copper stage, sedimentation may remove solids but cannot be assumed to remove dissolved copper or recover the organic substrate quantitatively.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible opening of the cyclic hemiaminal exposes a three-carbon guanidino aldehyde. Cyanide addition to its carbonyl and proton transfer generate the cyanohydrin, adding one carbon from HCN.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review describes ring opening under Patel et al. (2015). Carbonyl trapping through a ring-chain equilibrium is more defensible than direct cyanide displacement at a saturated hemiaminal carbon while retaining hydroxyl. Nevertheless, the equilibrium population, productive trapping rate, and substrate-specific selectivity are not established; this remains a conditional mechanistic interpretation.

reactions.name: Sulfide addition to the guanidino cyanohydrin nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9, substrate 0.1-5 mM, total dissolved sulfide 5-50 mM, 6-168 h. Use a shaded sulfide-bearing compartment and measure cyanohydrin dissociation, hydrolysis, and sulfur-containing side products.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrosulfide attacks the nitrile carbon. Proton transfers and tautomerization give the thioamide while retaining the adjacent hydroxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile thiolysis is the transformation described in the supplied review under Patel et al. (2015). Its reaction-class plausibility does not establish selectivity for this multifunctional substrate. Abundant Fe2+ can remove sulfide as iron sulfides, so sulfide availability must be measured rather than inferred from volcanic supply alone.

reactions.name: Unvalidated copper-consuming reductive deoxygenation
agents: Native copper, represented by mol_007, as a hypothetical stoichiometric reductant

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 6-9, substrate 0.1-5 mM, dissolved sulfide 1-20 mM, copper loading 4-20 equivalents, 1-72 h. Compare dark and 254 nm laboratory irradiation at 0.1-1 mW/cm2. Require measured organic mass balance, sulfur speciation, copper consumption, and passivation behavior before assigning productive conversion.

reactions.mechanism: The proposed net transformation replaces the alpha hydroxyl group with hydrogen and releases water. Two Cu atoms would supply two electrons by oxidation to Cu(I), with externally supplied sulfide captured as Cu2S. The elementary carbon-oxygen bond-cleavage mechanism is unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE and a major bottleneck. The supplied review attributes reductive dehydroxylation to Patel et al. (2015), but gives no substrate-specific mechanistic or yield evidence sufficient to validate it here. This is reduction, not dehydration alone, and it neither branches nor lengthens the carbon skeleton. Explicit copper consumption avoids attributing reduction to an unbalanced equation or an undefined Cu/H2S catalytic cycle. Atom balance still does not establish that this reaction occurs selectively.

reactions.name: Unvalidated reductive desulfurization of the thioamide to an aldehyde
agents: Native copper, represented by mol_007, as a hypothetical stoichiometric reductant and sulfur acceptor

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 4-8, substrate 0.1-5 mM, copper loading 4-20 equivalents, 1-72 h. No additional sulfide is required by this model. Test aldehyde formation and survival independently before attempting downstream capture. Transfer time, dissolved-metal carryover, and intermediate recovery are unmeasured.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized copper-mediated reductive sulfur removal gives an imine-level intermediate, followed by hydrolysis to the aldehyde and ammonia. Two Cu atoms become Cu(I) in Cu2S; the sulfur in this coproduct originates from the thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE and a major bottleneck. The review's combined thioamide-to-cyanohydrin step, attributed to Patel et al. (2015), conceals aldehyde-level reduction before HCN addition. Splitting these operations exposes the missing chemistry. Unlike a model in which H2S cancels and substrate sulfur is implicitly oxidized to elemental sulfur, this model assigns the electrons to copper oxidation and retains sulfur at oxidation state -II. Neither this sulfur fate nor selective aldehyde formation is established. Hydrolysis, overreduction, copper passivation, and intramolecular trapping of the aldehyde must be excluded experimentally.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation from 4-guanidinobutanal

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9, aldehyde 0.1-5 mM, HCN 5-50 mM, 0.5-24 h. Test capture immediately after aldehyde generation and compare with its independently measured decomposition and cyclization rates. No quantitative transfer recovery is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the accessible aldehyde carbonyl. Protonation of the alkoxide yields the five-carbon cyanohydrin backbone, with the guanidine carbon already present as the sixth carbon of the eventual target.
reactions.reasoning: Carbonyl cyanohydrin formation is chemically conventional and is the trapping component of the combined transformation attributed to Patel et al. (2015) in the supplied review. Application to 4-guanidinobutanal is conditional on obtaining an accessible open-chain aldehyde. Guanidination avoids the free 4-aminobutanal/proline-precursor problem, but does not eliminate possible guanidine-assisted cyclization or intermolecular condensation.

reactions.name: Strecker equilibration from cyanohydrin to arginine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.5-10, cyanohydrin 0.1-5 mM, total ammonia 0.1-1 M, 1-72 h. Maintain the cyanide-containing inventory while measuring volatilization, cyclic products, and aminonitrile formation. A shaded ammonia-rich stage is preferable to assuming compatibility with the preceding copper/sulfide mixture.

reactions.mechanism: The cyanohydrin reversibly releases aldehyde and HCN. Ammonia forms an imine or iminium species from the aldehyde, and cyanide trapping gives the alpha-aminonitrile. The net reaction releases water; it is not direct substitution of an unactivated hydroxyl group by ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: This is a corrected Strecker interpretation of the amination attributed to Patel et al. (2015) in the supplied review. No general C-N-versus-C-O bond-strength argument establishes its direction or yield. Carbonyl availability, ammonia/cyanide speciation, and competing cyclization control productive flux. Without a demonstrated chiral influence, both configurations at the new alpha carbon are expected.

reactions.name: Acid-catalyzed hydration of arginine aminonitrile to argininamide
agents: Hydronium ions from an acidic aqueous reservoir

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 0-1.5, substrate 0.1-10 mM, 1-14 days. Use a separate shaded acidic geothermal pool after sulfide/metal treatment. Measure aminonitrile, amide, acid, and side-chain degradation as a time course; the stated window does not establish complete conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Acid activation of the nitrile permits water addition and proton transfers to form the primary carboxamide. The guanidine and alpha-amino groups are predominantly protonated under these conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile hydration is the first part of the hydrolytic endgame described in the supplied review under Patel et al. (2015). Resolving the amide makes the kinetic requirement explicit. Acidic hydrolysis is chemically credible, but the supplied evidence does not establish conversion rates or selectivity for this aminonitrile. Delivery into a sufficiently acidic hot pool, dilution losses, and survival during transfer remain environmental requirements rather than demonstrated facts.

reactions.name: Acid-catalyzed argininamide hydrolysis to arginine
agents: Hydronium ions from an acidic aqueous reservoir

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 0-1, substrate 0.1-10 mM, 7-30 days, with time-resolved product analysis. These residence times are test windows, not measured completion times. Quantify guanidino-group retention and distinguish arginine from ornithine, other hydrolysis products, and residual amide.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the acid-activated amide carbonyl. Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate releases ammonia, present mainly as ammonium in the reaction medium, and forms the amino-acid carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Amide hydrolysis completes the nitrile-hydrolysis endgame attributed to Patel et al. (2015) by the supplied review. Together rxn_011 and rxn_012 consume two water molecules per aminonitrile without repeating molecule IDs in either reaction list. This conventional endpoint is preferable to assuming unverified hydantoin decarbamoylation, but selective completion below 370 K still requires experimental confirmation. The product is stereochemically unspecified arginine, not demonstrated enantiopure L-arginine.

pathways.name: Corrected early-guanidination candidate with explicit reductive bottlenecks
pathways.description: A single connected candidate from acetylene, HCN, ammonia, cyanamide, water, sulfide, and native copper to racemic arginine. Early guanidination precedes two carbon-chain extensions, and the final aminonitrile is hydrolyzed through an explicit amide. Reactions rxn_004, rxn_007, and rxn_008 are unvalidated gatekeeper hypotheses, so this sequence is not an established viable synthesis. The hypothetical redox model requires a total of six Cu atoms converted to three Cu2S units per arginine molecule before accounting for losses; catalytic copper turnover is not assumed. Only one pathway is listed because the supplied evidence does not justify the requested ten chemically distinct routes.

evaluation.target_molecule: Arginine, stereochemically unspecified; racemic product expected

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The proposed carbon-skeleton progression is coherent, and the endpoint is structurally consistent with racemic arginine. However, the complete route depends on three unresolved reductions. rxn_004 requires selective nitrile reduction to an aldehyde/hemiaminal rather than ordinary nitrile hydrolysis; rxn_007 requires deoxygenation while retaining the thioamide; and rxn_008 requires reductive thioamide conversion to an aldehyde. Formation of Cu2S closes their formal electron and atom balances but does not demonstrate that native copper performs these transformations selectively. Secondary concerns include the unspecified active Cu(I) catalyst in rxn_001, cyanamide guanidination selectivity in rxn_003, and substrate-specific equilibria in rxn_005 and rxn_010. The carbonyl-equilibrium and Strecker descriptions are chemically preferable to direct hydroxide displacement. The final hydration and amide hydrolysis are conventional transformations, but their plausibility cannot establish target production when essential upstream reactions remain unvalidated. These limitations establish uncertainty, not proof that the proposed reactions are impossible.
suggestions: Write the coefficient 2 explicitly for Cu in rxn_004, rxn_007 and rxn_008. These are balanceable equations, not conservation violations.
Prioritize substrate-specific validation of rxn_004, rxn_007 and rxn_008, including product identification, yields, competing products, copper oxidation states and inorganic sulfur products.

Specify reaction-specific pH, temperature, duration, concentration, pressure where relevant, and energy or redox requirements. Despite the strategy's reference to numerical screening windows, none are supplied.

Establish the source and speciation of the Cu(I) hydrocyanation catalyst. Assess copper consumption, sulfide-induced passivation and competition between cyanide, sulfide and organic substrates for copper.

Explain physically plausible staging between ammonia/sulfide-dependent chemistry and acidic final hydrolysis, including reagent carryover, volatile losses and any necessary separation or concentration.
Measure cyanamide guanidination selectivity, cyclic-hemiaminal/open-aldehyde partitioning, and cyanohydrin/imine/aminonitrile equilibria for the actual guanidino substrates.

Provide reaction-level primary references and distinguish reported transformations from new hypotheses. Confirm the integrated route by identifying and quantifying arginine while checking retention of its guanidino group.

evaluation.network_feedback: Network validity is strong: the 20 molecule nodes and 12 reaction nodes form a connected route with consistent identifiers and no isolated subgraphs. The deterministic check establishes nine reactions balanced as written and three balanceable with small coefficients; there are no conservation violations. Classifying terminal Cu2S as an intermediate is a schema limitation rather than a chemical defect. A single pathway is sufficient for evaluation, and no penalty is assigned for the absence of additional routes or environments. Environmental consistency remains under-specified: 'Surface' alone does not establish suitable catalyst speciation, reaction conditions or staging. Literature alignment is partial. The network appropriately corrects questionable mechanisms and acknowledges its decisive uncertainties, but the general Patel et al. citation (2015, DOI: 10.1038/nchem.2202) does not establish experimental support for the explicitly hypothetical Cu(0)-consuming reductions. The review's claim of a demonstrated complete arginine synthesis should be checked against the primary paper and supporting information. Overall confidence reflects the unresolved essential transformations, not an average of the more plausible individual steps. This is a conservation-consistent research candidate, not an approved complete synthesis network.
